## The reviewer's quoted values (CW-03)

- **C10 approx. 0.719 (COD10K-test) and 0.769 (NC4K):** our 3-seed SINet C10 means are 0.7185 and 0.7690 (per-run rows in Appendix D); at 8 seeds 0.7175 and 0.7684. SINet-v2 C10 is lower: 0.6952 and 0.7490 (8 seeds).
- **RISE 0.763 / 0.805:** RISE Table 1, row DINOv2-ViT-L14 (their strongest DINO configuration); our re-score of the released maps gives 0.7634 / 0.8053.
- **SINet-v2 approx. 0.815 / 0.847:** 0.815 is SINet-V2 Table 2 (COD10K); NC4K is not in the paper, and 0.847 matches our re-score of the officially released NC4K maps (0.8472).

## Correction to the initial rebuttal (RISE description)

The initial response described RISE as relying on "a different representation (frozen self-supervised ViT features with dataset-level retrieval) and a different training pipeline". The paper (Sec. 4.1, p.6) shows that RISE's detector **is SINet-V2**, trained with SINet-V2's own training process, on pseudo masks that RISE generates for **the same 4040 COD10K/CAMO training images** that our pipeline uses as its unlabelled target pool; the frozen DINOv2-ViT-L/14 features and retrieval are used only to generate those pseudo masks. The gap to RISE therefore isolates the *source of supervision on the target images* (RISE: pseudo masks on the real target images; ours: synthetic renders plus self-training) far more than a difference in detector or representation. EXP-03 E3-e (our trainer on RISE's released pseudo masks) measures this directly. Our clustering also uses frozen DINOv2 ViT-L/14 features, but only to allocate the synthetic budget.
